newsitem.title: FRANCE: Focus - French policy options unclear ahead of vote.
newsitem.headline: Focus - French policy options unclear ahead of vote.

text.p: France's voters could be facing anything from free-market liberalism to Communist-backed socialism on Monday after the left's upset win in the first round of a French parliamentary election.

The first-round lead by the combined left prompted Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose unpopularity has been blamed for the centre-right's poor showing on Sunday, to announce he would step down whichever party won the second-round runoff vote on June 1.

An official source said President Jacques Chirac was not expected to name any preference for his future prime minister before Sunday, leaving the choice wide open between the centre-right's liberal wing and more traditional politicians.

The Socialist party meanwhile declined to spell out any further the policy implications of its electoral pact with the Communists, in which only the leading candidate from either party will contest the second round against the right.
"If we win we will look at the question of government participation," Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande told a news conference.
Whoever wins, a commitment to European monetary union by all mainstream parties is expected to be the overriding factor determining French economic policies in the months ahead.
But how France gets there, and how deep any reforms might be to modernise the economy and reduce record unemployment at 12.8 percent may stay unanswered until after the final vote.
On the centre-right, Chirac would face a broad choice of candidates for prime minister.

They include National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, who campaigned against the Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum. Though he has since declared suppport for the euro single currency, he wants European policies geared to growth and employment.
Former prime minister Edouard Balladur, who has recently donned more economic liberal clothes, has also been tipped.

"It's an important strategic choice by the right to determine whether to go for market liberal policies and free-enterprise or reassure social protection will be maintained," Merrill Lynch economist Joanne Perez said.
On the left, the Socialist party said it would put the fight for jobs at the heart of its campaign, but said this was consistent with its commitment to monetary union.
"Let us say very clearly there will be no rise in income taxes and no rise in public spending," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said in a television interview.

The Socialists would combine "realistic necessity with a change in political direction to focus on the fight against unemployment", he said. "All that is coherent with our approach to European policy."

The Socialists have said they back a single currency but oppose any new austerity just to satisfy an "arithmetic interpretation" of a Maastricht treaty criterion limiting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.

But they have not said what concessions the party would make to the Communists in return for it swallowing its resistance to monetary union, although Jospin has said the Socialist line will prevail on Europe.

Hollande promised there was no risk of the Socialists making the kind of U-turn made by Chirac in October 1995, just five months after his election as president, when he put reducing the budget deficit above a campaign pledge to make fighting unemployment a priority.
But he declined to say what a Socialist government would do if it found on taking office that public finances were in a worse state than presented by the government.

Official sources have said the deficit may be running at anything between 20 and 40 billion francs ($3.5 billion and $7 billion) more than forecasts, although ministers say deficit reduction plans are on course.
The Socialists say they will carry out an audit of public finances if they win and seek a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty if France's deficit overshoots.
Hollande however acknowledged the Socialists may have to keep a 37.5-billion-franc windfall made this year for government accounts from a transfer of pension funds from state-owned France Telecom.

"If it was really necessary, it could be retained for a few years just to respect the (Maastricht treaty) criteria," he said, saying however the party disliked this kind of "accounting trick" to achieve European economic convergence. ($1 = 5.7 FFr)
